current.lab_name: The Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, Maine, USA)

story: Kevin Flurkey is a co-author of four Atlas papers from the National Institute on Aging Interventions Testing Program (ITP), which tests possible anti-aging drugs in genetically mixed mice at three sites at once. The 2009 Nature paper (HAR2009) showed that rapamycin, a drug that blocks mTOR, extended mouse lifespan even when it was started late in life. Follow-up papers showed that resveratrol and simvastatin did not extend life in the same experiment (MIL2011), that rapamycin's effect grows with dose and is larger in females (MIL2014), and that acarbose, 17-alpha-estradiol and NDGA extend lifespan mainly in males (HAR2014). These are mouse results; whether they carry over to people is still open.

Flurkey's PubMed record goes back to 1982, with a paper with Caleb Finch on how levels of the reproductive hormones LH, progesterone and prolactin change with age in female C57BL/6J mice. At The Jackson Laboratory, Flurkey has worked on mouse aging with David Harrison's group, including the ITP studies and, more recently, genetic studies of lifespan in Diversity Outbred mice, a genetically mixed mouse population. A 2025 paper in Genetics, with Gary Churchill's group and Calico Life Sciences, combined three such studies with 2,444 mice and found eight regions of the genome that affect lifespan.

current.lab_name: Heilongjiang Key Laboratory for Laboratory Animals and Comparative Medicine, College of Veterinary Medicine, Northeast Agricultural University (Harbin, China)
current.role: Veterinary toxicologist at Northeast Agricultural University in Harbin whose group studies how pollutants and food toxins damage the kidney, liver and gut in mice
current.sub: Heilongjiang Key Laboratory for Laboratory Animals and Comparative Medicine, College of Veterinary Medicine, Northeast Agricultural University, Harbin
story: Zheng Cao was senior author of a 2026 Environmental Science & Technology study (MIAO2026) on EDPrB, a liquid-crystal monomer, one of the chemicals used in flat screens that can leak into the environment. In mice, EDPrB built up in the kidney and caused chronic kidney disease. The team traced the harm to overactive mTOR, the cell's growth switch. When mTOR stays on, autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, is held back, and the kidney developed inflammation and fibrosis, a stiff scar tissue. Rapamycin, which blocks mTOR, prevented the damage, which marked mTOR activation as the first step in the chain. Human kidney cells grown in a dish gave matching results.

The study is written as an adverse outcome pathway, a step-by-step map from the first molecular hit to disease that toxicologists use to judge chemical risks. It is evidence from mice and cultured cells, not from exposed people.

Cao's group at the Heilongjiang Key Laboratory for Laboratory Animals and Comparative Medicine in Harbin works on how contaminants injure organs. Recent papers from the group show that the mycotoxin deoxynivalenol, a common contaminant of grain, breaks down the gut barrier (2024) and harms the liver through excessive mitophagy, the removal of mitochondria (2025), that the plastic chemical bisphenol F causes kidney inflammation and fibrosis through stress in the endoplasmic reticulum (2026), and that a berberine gel can ease mastitis in a mouse model (2026).

studies.title: Chronic Kidney Disease Risk Posed by 1-Ethoxy-2,3-difluoro-4-(trans-4-propylcyclohexyl) Benzene (EDPrB): An AOP of mTOR-Mediated Autophagy Dysregulation.

current.role: Toxicologist at Central China Normal University in Wuhan who leads mouse studies of how early-life exposure to microplastics, nanoplastics and plastic additives harms the developing brain
current.sub: Key Laboratory of Pesticide and Chemical Biology of the Ministry of Education and Hubei Key Laboratory of Genetic Regulation and Integrative Biology, School of Life Sciences, Central China Normal University
story: Rui Li is the senior (last) author of YANG2026. Young children take in tiny plastic particles from bottles, toys and food containers, often together with DEHP, a chemical that makes plastic soft. In this study, young mice exposed to polypropylene microplastics and DEHP developed brain and behaviour changes that resemble features of autism spectrum disorder, including reduced social behaviour. In their brains mTOR was overactive and autophagy, the cell's recycling system that mTOR normally restrains, was impaired. Treating the mice with rapamycin restored autophagy and improved the social and behavioural problems. The work is in mice, so it shows a possible mechanism, not proof that plastic exposure causes autism in children.

PubMed lists Li as senior author of a series of papers from the School of Life Sciences at Central China Normal University on plastic pollution and the young brain. In 2023 the group reported that combined exposure to polypropylene microplastics and DEHP caused memory problems, damage in the hippocampus and inflammation in young mice, through a long-lasting stress response in the protein-folding system. In 2025, in ACS Nano, the group showed that polystyrene nanoplastics disturb protein balance in the brain partly through changes in gut bacteria, with the sugar trehalose acting as a link between gut and brain.
Because Li is a very common surname, only papers from this Central China Normal University group were counted. No official profile could be checked, so academic rank and training are not given.

story: In the Atlas study BAN2014, Currie's group, with first author Christian Bannister, used UK primary care records to compare people with type 2 diabetes who started on metformin or on a sulphonylurea with matched people without diabetes. People started on metformin had slightly longer median survival than the matched non-diabetic group, while those on sulphonylureas had shorter survival. Metformin acts on the cell's energy sensing, which feeds into mTOR, and is being studied as a possible anti-ageing drug.

The result is observational. Differences between the patients that the records do not capture, and the tendency of people who take their medicine to be healthier in other ways, could explain part of it. It is consistent with a benefit but does not prove one.

On PubMed, Currie is the senior author on a long line of studies from Cardiff University using the Clinical Practice Research Datalink, a large database of anonymised GP records, on diabetes drugs, cardiovascular risk and survival. A 2023 paper lists him at both the Division of Population Medicine in Cardiff University's School of Medicine and Human Data Sciences in Cardiff, on a platform that produces disease statistics from routine health records almost in real time.

story: Jun Zhang is the senior and corresponding author of the Atlas study SU2026, with Yanhong Su as first author. The study looked at heart damage that happens when blood flow returns after a heart artery has been blocked, known as ischemia-reperfusion injury. Some of the heart cells die by necroptosis, a programmed form of cell death in which the cell bursts open.

The team focused on DLX6-AS1, a long non-coding RNA (an RNA that regulates other genes but does not code for a protein). Its level rose in injured mouse hearts. In rat heart cells put through oxygen loss and return, more DLX6-AS1 switched on PI3K, AKT and mTOR and increased necroptosis, and blocking it reduced the damage. The results come from mice and a cell line, so they point to a possible drug target rather than a treatment.

PubMed lists Zhang at the Department of Cardiology of Cangzhou Central Hospital in Hebei province, which is affiliated with Tianjin Medical University. Jun Zhang is a very common name, and no official page could be matched with confidence, so this profile rests on the affiliation given on the Atlas paper.

story: Xiaoyan Zhang is the senior author of a 2026 study on kidney fibrosis, the scarring that slowly destroys function in chronic kidney disease. The team, with Shiqi Lv as first author, described a chain of control. The enzyme USP7 removes destruction tags from KDM5B, an enzyme that edits the chemical marks on DNA packaging proteins. Stable KDM5B shuts down the gene for TSC1, one half of the main brake on mTOR, and mTOR activity then rises and promotes scarring.

Blocking USP7, by deleting it or with a drug, brought TSC1 back, lowered mTOR activity and reduced fibrosis in two mouse models of kidney injury. In human kidney biopsies USP7 was higher in chronic kidney disease and rose with the amount of scarring, which is an association rather than proof of cause. The authors propose the USP7-KDM5B-TSC1-mTOR axis as a possible drug target.

PubMed gives the Department of Nephrology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University, Shanghai, as the affiliation. Because Xiaoyan Zhang is a very common name, no wider publication record or career details are given here without a second independent link.

studies.title: Deubiquitinase USP7 stabilizes the histone demethylase KDM5B and promotes the progression of renal fibrosis through the TSC1/mTOR axis

story: In 2002 two teams, one in Boston and one in Kobe, reported raptor, the partner protein that defines mTORC1, the growth-control complex. Sujuti Hidayat is a co-author of the Kobe paper in Cell (HARA2002). It showed that raptor is needed for mTOR to act on 4E-BP1 and S6 kinase, two proteins that control protein synthesis, and that silencing raptor in the worm C. elegans mimics loss of TOR. Hidayat is also a co-author of the 2003 follow-up (NOJ2003) showing that raptor holds these targets through a short TOS motif.

Hidayat's own first-author paper from the same group, published in 2003, tested a chemical cousin of the amino acid leucine. It blocked the amino acid signal to mTOR in human Jurkat cells, a line of immune cells, and stopped them in the G1 phase of the cell cycle. That study lists Hidayat at the Biosignal Research Center of Kobe University.

PubMed records place Hidayat in the Yonezawa group from 2000 to 2006, on papers about the tail region of mTOR that the enzyme needs to work (2000), about how the Hsp90 inhibitor geldanamycin disrupts the mTOR-raptor pathway (2006), and about the two motifs of 4E-BP1 that bind raptor (2006). story: Kristin Moreth is a co-author on two Atlas studies that relied on large-scale mouse phenotyping, the systematic measuring of many body functions in the same animals. EIS2016 showed that oral spermidine, a natural compound also found in food, lengthened the lives of mice, kept heart muscle from thickening and kept the heart able to relax normally between beats. The benefit disappeared in mice whose heart muscle cells lack the autophagy gene Atg5, so autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, was needed for the effect. The paper also included a human diet survey linking spermidine intake to lower blood pressure and fewer heart problems, but that part is observational and cannot show cause. NEF2013 gave rapamycin, the drug that blocks mTOR, to young and old mice and measured a very wide panel of body functions. Rapamycin lengthened life but changed only a few of the classic signs of ageing, so a longer life did not mean that ageing slowed down across the whole body. Both are mouse studies.

Moreth is listed at the German Mouse Clinic in Neuherberg, near Munich, on 34 PubMed papers. The German Mouse Clinic at Helmholtz Munich tests mouse models in a standardised way across many organ systems; its recent papers cover heart size, movement, behaviour, metabolism and blood values. The most recent, from 2021, used the clinic's heart phenotyping in a study of the gene Creld1, which mice need for normal development of the heart muscle. A later position could not be confirmed.

story: Nicola Zamboni is a co-author of two Atlas studies that measured cell metabolism. story: Yuji Ikeno is a co-author of two Atlas papers on ageing. LAB2015, from Judith Campisi's group, studied senescent cells, old cells that stop dividing but keep releasing inflammatory signals called the SASP. These signals can harm nearby tissue and even help tumours grow. The team showed that mTOR drives the SASP by boosting the production of IL1A, the signal at the top of the cascade, and that rapamycin turned this off and stopped senescent cells from feeding prostate tumour growth in mice. DUR2026, from John Kopchick's group, deleted the growth hormone receptor in mice at 12 months of age, which is middle age for a mouse. The mice still lived longer, in both sexes, and the males kept better insulin sensitivity, muscle performance and bone. This matters because most growth-hormone longevity mice lack the hormone signal from birth, while this study shows that a midlife start is still enough.

PubMed lists Ikeno on more than 120 papers on ageing, many of them from the Barshop Institute in San Antonio, where the long-lived mouse models and anti-ageing drug studies need careful pathology to show what the animals died of and which diseases were delayed. In both Atlas papers the role is consistent with this: examining tissues from the mice.

story: mTORC2 is the second mTOR complex. It controls the kinase Akt, cell survival and the cell skeleton, and unlike mTORC1 it is not blocked by rapamycin. In 2018 Edward Stuttfeld was first author of an eLife paper, with senior authors Nenad Ban and Timm Maier, that used cryo-electron microscopy to show how the four core parts of human mTORC2 (mTOR, Rictor, SIN1 and mLST8) fit together. The structure helped explain why rapamycin does not act on mTORC2. A 2020 follow-up at 3.2 angstrom resolution, on which Stuttfeld is a co-author, pinned this to the tail end of Rictor. These are protein structure studies.

Stuttfeld began in vascular biology. With Kurt Ballmer-Hofer at the Paul Scherrer Institut in Villigen, Stuttfeld wrote a 2009 review on VEGF receptors, the receptors for a growth factor that drives blood-vessel growth, and later co-authored structural studies of VEGF receptors 1, 2 and 3.

In Timm Maier's group at the Biozentrum, Stuttfeld worked on large enzymes and signalling complexes. Besides the mTORC2 papers, Stuttfeld co-authored a 2018 Nature structure of human acetyl-CoA carboxylase, the first enzyme of fatty acid synthesis, and a 2021 eLife study of how DEPTOR binds and regulates both mTOR complexes. A current position could not be confirmed.

story: Ofer Moldavski is a co-author of two Zoncu lab papers in this Atlas. Every cell has to decide whether it has enough raw materials to grow. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, makes that decision on the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, where it is switched on when nutrients are present. Amino acids were the best-known signal; CAS2017 showed that cholesterol inside the lysosome is another one. SLC38A9, a transporter-like protein already known to sense the amino acid arginine, is needed for cholesterol to switch mTORC1 on, and it uses separate cholesterol-responsive parts of the protein to do it. NPC1, the protein that moves cholesterol out of the lysosome and is faulty in Niemann-Pick type C disease, binds SLC38A9 and holds mTORC1 back. The experiments used cell lines and fibroblasts from patients, not whole animals. LAW2018 looked at the scaffold that holds the Rag GTPases on the lysosome, a protein complex called Ragulator. It found that nutrients change how tightly the Rags bind this scaffold, a switch that controls whether mTORC1 is pulled to the lysosome and turned on.

Moldavski was first author of a 2021 Journal of Lipid Research paper, with affiliations at UC Berkeley and the Cardiovascular Research Institute at UCSF. It reported that 4beta-hydroxycholesterol, an oxidised form of cholesterol, promotes fat production by switching on the master regulator SREBP1c through the liver X receptor.
No current position could be confirmed with certainty, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas papers.

story: Fission yeast is a single-celled fungus used to study how cells control growth. Its TORC1 complex is the yeast version of mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and it can be blocked with rapamycin plus caffeine. Lufeng Dan is first author of the 2026 Microbiology Spectrum study in this Atlas (DAN2026). Some yeast cells became resistant to the drugs, then lost the resistance again a few generations later. The team showed that this was not an epigenetic switch. Mutations that broke the gaf1 gene appeared under drug pressure and then reverted to the normal DNA sequence when the drug was gone. Gaf1 is a GATA transcription factor that slows growth downstream of TORC1. The authors warn that such hidden switches can quietly change laboratory yeast stocks.

The paper continues a line of work Dan began at the Life Sciences Institute of Zhejiang University in Hangzhou, in the group of Xiangwei He. A 2021 PNAS paper with Dan as first author found drug-resistance mutations in fission yeast that are made by short tandem duplications of DNA and then flip back to the original sequence, and used deep genome sequencing to find thousands of such duplications in a single population.

By 2025 Dan was at the School of Pharmacy of Chengdu University, where a paper in the Chinese journal Hereditas described a screen that isolated 14 yeast strains with unstable rapamycin resistance, again with Xiangwei He as a co-author.

studies.title: Recurrent reversible mutations at gaf1 driving metastable TORC1 inhibitor resistance in fission yeast.

story: Aykut Demir was first author of a 2026 paper in Blood (DEM2026) about acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), a fast-growing blood cancer. AML returns after treatment because a small group of leukaemic stem cells survives. These cells depend on the TCA cycle, the chain of reactions in mitochondria that burns fuel for energy, more than healthy blood stem cells do. The team found that the enzyme IDH3, one step of that cycle, is more abundant in leukaemic stem cells.

When they lowered IDH3A, the working part of the enzyme, citrate piled up inside the cells and both main energy pathways slowed. The resulting energy shortage switched on AMPK, the cell's fuel gauge, which shut down mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and so cut protein production. The cells then became more sensitive to venetoclax, a drug that blocks the survival protein BCL2. Healthy blood formation was spared. The work used patient cells, bone marrow organoids (miniature lab-grown tissue) and mice, and in a patient group, stem cells from people whose leukaemia resisted venetoclax plus azacitidine showed gene programmes of an active TCA cycle.

The paper lists Demir at Heidelberg University, in a team led by Simon Raffel at Heidelberg University Hospital with Andreas Trumpp of the German Cancer Research Center and Carsten Müller-Tidow among the co-authors. Other PubMed records under the same initials belong to different people, and a fuller career history could not be confirmed.

studies.title: IDH3 regulates citrate homeostasis to control metabolic fitness and venetoclax resistance of AML stem cells

current.role: Neuroscience researcher in Sean Cregan's lab at Western University who showed that chronic ATF4 stress signalling shuts down mTOR and kills dopamine neurons in models of Parkinson's disease
current.sub: Neuroscience Program, Schulich School of Medicine and Dentistry, and Robarts Research Institute, University of Western Ontario (Sean Cregan lab, papers 2020–2026)
story: In Parkinson's disease the dopamine-making neurons of the midbrain die. Matthew Demmings' 2026 paper in Cell Reports (DEMMINGS2026), from Sean Cregan's lab at Western University in Canada, traced one route to that death. In cell and animal models of the disease, a long-lasting stress response called the integrated stress response kept the transcription factor ATF4 active. ATF4 turned up three genes, SESN2, DDIT4 and TRIB3, whose proteins together lowered the activity of both mTOR complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2. That sustained loss of mTOR signalling switched on PUMA, a protein that triggers cell suicide, and the neurons died.

Much of the ageing literature treats lower mTOR activity as good. This study is a reminder that neurons need some mTOR signalling to survive, and that chronic shutdown can be harmful. The results come from cell and animal models, not from patients.

The paper builds on Demmings' earlier first-author study from the same lab, published in Cell Death and Differentiation in 2020, which showed that ATF4 promotes the death of neurons exposed to Parkinson's toxins and to clumps of the protein alpha-synuclein. In 2025 Demmings was also first author of a review on how neurons and glial cells interact from brain development to disease, and a co-author of a review on metabolic networks in the healthy brain.

studies.title: ATF4 activates a transcriptional program that chronically suppresses mTOR activity and promotes neurodegeneration in Parkinson disease models

current.lab_name: School of Pharmacy, Lanzhou University (Lanzhou, China)
current.role: Pharmacy researcher at Lanzhou University working with Wen Li on the chemistry and actions of traditional Chinese medicines, from extracting plant compounds to testing a herbal formula in breast cancer models
current.sub: School of Pharmacy, Lanzhou University (papers with Wen Li, 2024–2026; at the time of the study)
story: Jingyue Zhang was first author of a 2026 Atlas study on the Xingxiao Pill, a traditional Chinese herbal formula, in breast cancer models (ZHANG2026C). The pill slowed the growth of 4T1 mouse breast cancer cells in culture and of 4T1 tumours in mice. It lowered signalling along the ErbB3/PI3K/AKT/mTOR chain, a relay that carries growth signals from the cell surface down to mTOR, the cell's growth-control kinase, and it changed how the tumours used amino acids. Computer docking pointed to two of the pill's ingredients, cinnamic acid and palmitic acid, as compounds that can bind mTOR. All of this was done in mouse cells and mice, so it does not show an effect in patients.

Zhang's other papers from the School of Pharmacy at Lanzhou University, also with Wen Li as senior author, are on the chemistry side of plant medicines. A 2024 study in Food Chemistry, for example, built magnetic molecularly imprinted polymers, a kind of chemical trap shaped to fit one molecule, to pull the compound glabridin out of licorice waste left over from industrial processing.
No personal institutional page was found, so the position shown is the Lanzhou University affiliation on the Atlas paper.

studies.title: Anti-breast cancer effects of the Xingxiao Pill are associated with inhibition of the ErbB3/PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, modulation of amino acid metabolism, and promotion of apoptosis.

previous_note: Common name. PubMed also has a Jingyue Zhang at Xi'an Jiaotong University (PMID 42323314) who is a different person or cannot be tied; not used.

current.lab_name: Key Laboratory of Efficient Utilization of Non-grain Feed Resources, College of Animal Science and Technology, Shandong Agricultural University (Tai'an, Shandong, China)
current.role: Animal nutrition researcher in Ning Jiao's group at Shandong Agricultural University who studies how feed contaminants damage the pig gut, and first author of the piglet study on glutamine and bisphenol A
current.sub: College of Animal Science and Technology, Shandong Agricultural University (Ning Jiao group, papers 2026)
story: Bisphenol A (BPA) is an industrial chemical found in some plastics that can reach animal feed. In the Atlas study XIE2026, Xie, Ning Jiao and colleagues fed piglets BPA and found damage to the jejunum, the middle part of the small intestine. Adding the amino acid glutamine to the feed reduced the damage, helped the gut lining stay sealed and restored how the cells' mitochondria produce energy. These changes came with shifts in AMPK and mTOR signalling, the two linked sensors of cell energy and nutrients.
The study shows an association between glutamine, gut repair and AMPK-mTOR signalling in pigs. It does not prove that the mTOR change causes the protection, and it was not done in people.

PubMed lists Xie only in 2026, both times in Jiao's group at the Key Laboratory of Efficient Utilization of Non-grain Feed Resources at Shandong Agricultural University in Tai'an. The second paper looked at how the mould toxin zearalenone and its hidden glucoside form harm pig intestinal cells. The career stage (student or staff) could not be confirmed.

studies.title: Glutamine alleviates bisphenol A-induced jejunal injury in piglets involving mitochondrial function restoration and AMPK-mTOR signaling regulation.

previous_note: Common surname (Xie): identity tied by Shandong Agricultural University plus co-author Ning Jiao. No web profile found (web search budget ran out).

current.lab_name: Mockett Lab, Department of Biomedical Sciences, University of South Alabama (Mobile, Alabama, USA)
current.role: Researcher in Robin Mockett's lab at the University of South Alabama who showed that rapamycin's effect on fruit fly lifespan swings from harmful to helpful depending on the food
current.sub: Department of Biomedical Sciences, University of South Alabama (at the time of the 2026 study)
story: Lauren Jackson is the first author of JAC2026, a GeroScience paper from Robin Mockett's lab at the University of South Alabama. Rapamycin, which blocks mTORC1, is often described as a drug that lengthens life in many animals. This fruit fly (Drosophila) study tested that claim carefully across five fly strains, both sexes and two kinds of food.

The answer depended on the diet. On a cornmeal and torula yeast food, rapamycin shortened life in 19 of 26 experiments. On a richer brewer's yeast food it helped in 8 experiments, made no difference in 14, and never caused clear harm. Changes in median lifespan ranged from a 51 percent loss to a 5 percent gain and varied with sex and strain. Rapamycin was also toxic to developing flies at higher doses. The lesson for a reader is that a lifespan result in one lab, on one food, may not carry over to other conditions. It is a fly study, so it says nothing direct about people.
PubMed shows only this paper under this name with Mockett, and no official profile was found, so the position shown is the affiliation on the Atlas paper.

studies.title: Diet-dependent, beneficial and adverse effects of rapamycin on life span of Drosophila melanogaster

current.lab_name: Department of Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Shanxi Medical University (Taiyuan, Shanxi, China)
current.role: Toxicology and environmental health researcher who found that the long non-coding RNA LINP1 protects skin cells from radiation-induced senescence by binding mTOR
current.sub: Department of Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Shanxi Medical University (2026) · Department of Toxicology, School of Public Health, Southern Medical University, Guangzhou (2025)
story: Xiaoting Liang is first author of the Atlas study LIANG2026, with Liang Zhou of Southern Medical University in Guangzhou as senior author. Radiotherapy often damages the skin, and part of that damage comes from senescence, the state in which cells stop dividing for good. The team found that LINP1, a long non-coding RNA (an RNA that regulates other molecules without making a protein), rises sharply in keratinocytes, the main cells of the outer skin, after radiation.

LINP1 binds the FAT domain of mTOR through a central stretch of the RNA. This weakens the contact between mTOR and the tumour suppressor p53, so less p53 is phosphorylated at serine 15, and the cells are less likely to become senescent. Removing LINP1 made radiation damage worse in cultured keratinocytes and in pieces of human skin kept alive in the lab. Here mTOR acts as a partner of p53 in the stress response, not as a nutrient sensor.

Before moving to Shanxi Medical University in Taiyuan, Liang was listed at the Department of Toxicology of Southern Medical University's School of Public Health, as a co-author with Zhou on a 2025 study of how another long non-coding RNA drives drug resistance in melanoma.

studies.title: LINP1 suppresses radiation-induced cellular senescence in keratinocytes by modulating the mTOR-p53 axis

current.lab_name: Lamming Lab, Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison (Madison, Wisconsin, USA)
current.role: Researcher in Dudley Lamming's lab at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who studies how restricting single amino acids in the diet affects metabolism, memory and Alzheimer's disease in mice
current.sub: Graduate Program in Cellular and Molecular Biology and Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison (Lamming lab, papers from 2022) · earlier: Department of Surgery and Department of Pediatric Gastroenterology, Medical College of Wisconsin, and Aurora Research Institute, Milwaukee (papers 2012–2021)
story: Reji Babygirija was first author of a 2026 Advanced Science paper in this Atlas (BAB2025), first posted as a preprint. Branched-chain amino acids, leucine, isoleucine and valine, are building blocks of protein, and they act differently on mTORC1, the growth-control complex: leucine is a strong activator. The study restricted each of the three separately in 3xTg mice, a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. The effects on memory and Alzheimer's-type brain changes were distinct for each amino acid and differed between males and females. Cutting isoleucine or valine, but not leucine, improved metabolic health. The results come from mice and point to diet composition, not just total protein, as something that matters.

Before joining Lamming's group, Babygirija worked at the Medical College of Wisconsin in Milwaukee. As first author of a 2012 Brain Research paper from Takahashi's group in the Department of Surgery, Babygirija showed in rats that social interaction softened stress responses after chronic stress in animals separated from their mothers early in life. Later papers from Milwaukee covered visceral pain after bladder inflammation in young rats (2017), irritable bowel symptoms in inflammatory bowel disease (2019) and electro-acupuncture against chronic stress (2021).

At the University of Wisconsin-Madison, in the graduate program in cellular and molecular biology, Babygirija has co-authored many of the Lamming lab's diet studies, including a 2022 Cell Metabolism paper showing that sex and genetic background shape how mice respond to protein restriction. PubMed lists more than 60 papers with the name.

studies.title: Restriction of individual branched-chain amino acids has distinct effects on the development and progression of Alzheimer's disease in 3xTg mice

current.lab_name: Department of Occupational Health and Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Anhui Medical University (Hefei, China)
current.role: Environmental health researcher at Anhui Medical University and first author of a 2026 mouse study on how the solvent trichloroethylene damages the liver when the LKB1/AMPK energy sensor is missing
current.sub: Department of Occupational Health and Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Anhui Medical University (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Trichloroethylene is an industrial solvent used to degrease metal, and workers exposed to it can develop liver injury. Lifu Zhu's 2026 study, with J. Zhang as senior author, asked why some livers are hit harder. The focus was LKB1 and AMPK, a pair of enzymes that sense low energy in the cell and normally hold mTOR in check.

In mice lacking LKB1/AMPK, trichloroethylene caused worse liver injury. mTOR-regulated mitophagy, the clean-up of damaged mitochondria, failed, and mitochondrial DNA leaked out of the mitochondria, where it can trigger inflammation. Rapamycin, which blocks mTOR, and drugs that activate AMPK protected the liver. The work is in mice only, with no human data, and suggests the LKB1/AMPK/mTOR axis as a possible target.

PubMed lists Lifu Zhu at the Department of Occupational Health and Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Anhui Medical University in Hefei. A current position could not be confirmed from an official page.

studies.title: LKB1/AMPK deficiency aggravates mitochondrial DNA leakage via mTOR-dependent mitophagy damage in liver injury sensitized by trichloroethylene.

current.lab_name: Department of Plastic Surgery, The First Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University (Wenzhou, China)
current.role: Researcher in plastic surgery at Wenzhou Medical University and first author of a mouse study on engineered stem-cell exosomes that speed wound healing by changing fibroblast metabolism
current.sub: Department of Plastic Surgery, The First Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University (2026, at the time of the study)
story: Chronic wounds, such as foot ulcers in people with diabetes, can stay open for months. In the Atlas study CHEN2026 in Cellular Signalling, Kewei Chen was first author. The team engineered adipose-derived stem cells, stem cells taken from fat tissue, so that the tiny vesicles they release (exosomes) carried FGF21, a hormone that affects energy use. When these exosomes were given to skin fibroblasts, the cells that rebuild tissue, the fibroblasts switched up glycolysis, the quick sugar-burning pathway, with the energy sensor AMPK turned on and mTOR signalling turned down. The fibroblasts divided and moved faster, and wounds in a mouse model closed sooner. The evidence comes from cells and mice.

PubMed lists Chen in the Department of Plastic Surgery at the First Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University, with Li L as senior author. Because the name is very common, no other paper could be tied to this person with confidence, and no official profile page was found.

studies.title: FGF21-modified adipose stem cell-derived exosomes promote wound healing by activating fibroblast glycolysis through AMPK/mTOR signaling.

current.lab_name: Department of Pathology, University of Southern California (Los Angeles, California, USA)
current.role: Researcher in integrative medicine and nutrition science, trained at George Washington University, who wrote a cautious review of whether off-label rapamycin is justified for healthy adults
current.sub: Department of Pathology, University of Southern California (2026 paper) · earlier at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences (2025)
story: Jacob Hands was first author of a 2025 review in Aging (HAN2025) that asked a direct question: what does the human evidence say about taking low-dose rapamycin, or related mTOR-blocking drugs, to slow aging in healthy adults? Some people already take rapamycin off-label for this reason, based mostly on animal studies in which it lengthened life. The review collected the clinical studies and re-analysed one group of people using PhenoAge, a 'biological age' score calculated from routine blood tests.

Its verdict was careful. The animal data on lifespan are strong, but the human studies are small, short and use different doses and measures, and they have not shown that rapamycin slows aging in healthy people. The review is useful as a reminder of the gap between results in mice and evidence in people.

PubMed lists Hands at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences on the 2025 review. A 2026 narrative review in Nutrients, on common genetic variants that affect blood fats and heart disease risk and how diet might interact with them, lists Hands at the Department of Pathology of the University of Southern California, with co-authors from George Washington University's Office of Integrative Medicine and Health. No personal page was found to confirm job title or training.

studies.title: What is the clinical evidence to support off-label rapamycin therapy in healthy adults?

previous_note: Move from GWU to USC is based on the 2026 Nutrients affiliation only (same full name, GWU co-authors); role at USC unknown.
